blocks.body:
Asking for the second coordinate of a vector, evaluating a polynomial at $x=3$, and integrating a function over $[0,1]$ all do the same kind of thing: they take a vector and produce a number, linearly. Such maps are linear functionals, and collecting them gives a new vector space, the dual space. It is the natural home of "measurements" of vectors.

The second construction on this page goes the other way. Sometimes part of a space is irrelevant: we care about polynomials only through their value at $1$, or about vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ only up to adding multiples of a fixed direction. The quotient space formalises "work in $V$ but treat the subspace $U$ as zero". Duality and quotients turn out to be closely tied, and both rest on [[linear-maps|rank–nullity]].

blocks.title: Dual space
blocks.body:
Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$. A linear functional on $V$ is a linear map $\varphi: V \to F$. The dual space $V^* = \mathcal{L}(V, F)$ is the set of all linear functionals, a vector space under $(\varphi+\psi)(v) = \varphi(v)+\psi(v)$ and $(c\varphi)(v) = c\,\varphi(v)$.

On $F^n$, every functional has the form $\varphi(x) = a_1x_1+\dots+a_nx_n$, so functionals are row vectors and vectors are column vectors.

blocks.title: Dual basis
blocks.body: Let $v_1, \dots, v_n$ be a basis of $V$. Define $\varphi_j \in V^*$ by $\varphi_j(v_k) = 1$ if $j=k$ and $0$ otherwise. Then $\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n$ is a basis of $V^*$, called the dual basis, and every $\varphi \in V^*$ satisfies $\varphi = \sum_j \varphi(v_j)\,\varphi_j$. In particular $\dim V^* = \dim V$.

A linear map is determined by its values on a basis, and any values can be prescribed; so each $\varphi_j$ exists and is unique. Given $\varphi$, the functionals $\varphi$ and $\sum_j \varphi(v_j)\varphi_j$ agree on each $v_k$, hence everywhere; so the $\varphi_j$ span. If $\sum_j c_j\varphi_j = 0$, applying it to $v_k$ gives $c_k = 0$; so they are independent.

blocks.title: Computing dual bases
blocks.body:
Note that $\varphi_j(v)$ is just the $j$-th coordinate of $v$ in the basis $v_1,\dots,v_n$. In $F^n$ this gives a recipe: put the basis vectors as the columns of a matrix $B$; the coordinates of $x$ are $B^{-1}x$, so the dual basis functionals are the rows of $B^{-1}$.

For example take $v_1 = (1,1)$ and $v_2=(1,2)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Then $B = \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, $B^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}$, and $\varphi_1(x,y) = 2x-y$, $\varphi_2(x,y) = -x+y$. Check: $\varphi_1(1,1)=1$, $\varphi_1(1,2)=0$, $\varphi_2(1,1)=0$, $\varphi_2(1,2)=1$.

The same recipe shows a subtle point: $\varphi_1$ depends on the whole basis, not just on $v_1$. With the basis $(1,1),(0,1)$ instead, the first dual functional becomes $\varphi_1(x,y)=x$.

blocks.title: Annihilator
blocks.body:
For a subspace $U \subseteq V$, the annihilator is $U^0 = \{\varphi \in V^* : \varphi(u) = 0 \text{ for all } u \in U\}$, a subspace of $V^*$. If $V$ is finite-dimensional then $\dim U + \dim U^0 = \dim V$.

Meaning: a $k$-dimensional subspace of an $n$-dimensional space is cut out by exactly $n-k$ independent linear equations.

blocks.title: Proof of the dimension formula
blocks.body: Extend a basis $u_1,\dots,u_m$ of $U$ to a basis $u_1,\dots,u_m,v_{m+1},\dots,v_n$ of $V$, with dual basis $\varphi_1,\dots,\varphi_n$. Call these basis vectors $w_1,\dots,w_n$ (so $w_i = u_i$ for $i\le m$). If $\varphi \in U^0$ then $\varphi = \sum_j \varphi(w_j)\,\varphi_j$ and the first $m$ coefficients vanish, so $\varphi \in \operatorname{span}(\varphi_{m+1},\dots,\varphi_n)$. Conversely each $\varphi_j$ with $j>m$ kills all $u_i$. So $U^0$ has basis $\varphi_{m+1},\dots,\varphi_n$ and dimension $n-m$.

blocks.title: The dual map and the transpose
blocks.body:
A linear map $T: V \to W$ induces a map the other way, $T': W^* \to V^*$, by $T'(\psi) = \psi \circ T$: to measure $v$, first push it to $W$ and measure there. One checks directly that $(ST)' = T'S'$.

If $V, W$ have bases with dual bases, and $A$ is the matrix of $T$, then the matrix of $T'$ is the transpose $A^{\mathsf{T}}$: the $(k,j)$ entry of the matrix of $T'$ is $T'(\psi_j)(v_k) = \psi_j(Tv_k) = A_{jk}$. This is the conceptual meaning of the transpose.

Two facts follow quickly. First, $\operatorname{null} T' = (\operatorname{range} T)^0$, because $\psi\circ T = 0$ means precisely that $\psi$ vanishes on the range of $T$. Second, by rank–nullity for $T'$ and the annihilator formula,
$$\dim\operatorname{range} T' = \dim W - \dim(\operatorname{range} T)^0 = \dim \operatorname{range} T.$$
Read through matrices, this says that $A^{\mathsf{T}}$ and $A$ have the same rank: row rank equals column rank.

blocks.title: The double dual
blocks.body:
There is no natural isomorphism $V \to V^*$: the dual basis construction depends on a choice of basis. But there is a natural map $\Lambda: V \to V^{**}$, given by $\Lambda(v)(\varphi) = \varphi(v)$, "evaluate at $v$". It is injective, since for $v\neq 0$ we can extend $v$ to a basis and the first dual functional gives $\varphi(v) = 1$. In finite dimensions $\dim V^{**} = \dim V$, so $\Lambda$ is an isomorphism, and it requires no choices.

In infinite dimensions the dual is genuinely bigger. For $V = \mathbb{Q}[x]$, a functional may take arbitrary values on $1, x, x^2, \dots$, so $V^*$ is the space of all sequences of rationals; it has uncountable dimension while $V$ has countable dimension. The coefficient functionals $p \mapsto (\text{coefficient of } x^n)$ are independent but do not span: $p \mapsto p(1)$ is not a finite combination of them.

blocks.title: Quotient space
blocks.body:
Let $U$ be a subspace of $V$. For $v \in V$, the coset $v + U = \{v+u : u \in U\}$. The quotient space $V/U$ is the set of cosets, with $(v+U)+(w+U) = (v+w)+U$ and $c(v+U) = cv+U$. The quotient map $\pi: V\to V/U$ is $\pi(v) = v+U$.

Two cosets are equal, $v+U = w+U$, exactly when $v-w \in U$; the operations are well defined because changing $v$ and $w$ by elements of $U$ changes $v+w$ and $cv$ by elements of $U$. Geometrically, $\mathbb{R}^3/\text{(a line)}$ is the set of lines parallel to it, which behaves like a plane.

blocks.title: First isomorphism theorem and dimension of a quotient
blocks.body: If $T: V \to W$ is linear, then $\tilde T(v + \operatorname{null}T) = Tv$ is a well-defined isomorphism $V/\operatorname{null}T \to \operatorname{range} T$. If $V$ is finite-dimensional, $\dim V/U = \dim V - \dim U$, and $(V/U)^* \cong U^0$ via $\varphi \mapsto \varphi\circ\pi$.

If $v + \operatorname{null}T = v' + \operatorname{null}T$ then $v-v' \in \operatorname{null}T$, so $Tv = Tv'$: $\tilde T$ is well defined, and it is clearly linear and onto $\operatorname{range}T$. If $\tilde T(v+\operatorname{null}T) = 0$ then $v\in\operatorname{null}T$, so the coset is zero: $\tilde T$ is injective.

The quotient map $\pi$ is linear and onto with null space $U$, so rank–nullity gives $\dim V = \dim U + \dim V/U$. Finally, $\varphi \mapsto \varphi\circ\pi$ is linear and injective (as $\pi$ is onto), its image lies in $U^0$, and every $\psi \in U^0$ arises because $\psi$ is constant on cosets and hence defines a functional on $V/U$.

blocks.title: Simpson's rule from a dual basis
blocks.body: On the space $\mathcal{P}_2$ of real polynomials of degree at most $2$, let $e_k(p) = p(k)$ for $k=0,1,2$. Show that $e_0,e_1,e_2$ is a basis of $\mathcal{P}_2^*$, find the basis of $\mathcal{P}_2$ it is dual to, and write the functional $I(p) = \int_0^2 p(x)\,dx$ in this basis.
blocks.solution:
The polynomials
$$L_0 = \tfrac12(x-1)(x-2),\qquad L_1 = -x(x-2),\qquad L_2 = \tfrac12 x(x-1)$$
satisfy $L_j(k) = 1$ if $j=k$ and $0$ otherwise, i.e. $e_k(L_j) = \delta_{jk}$. They are independent (apply $e_k$ to a vanishing combination), so they form a basis of the $3$-dimensional $\mathcal{P}_2$, and $e_0,e_1,e_2$ is exactly its dual basis. By the dual basis theorem, $I = I(L_0)e_0 + I(L_1)e_1 + I(L_2)e_2$. Integrating, $I(L_0) = \tfrac13$, $I(L_1) = \tfrac43$, $I(L_2) = \tfrac13$, so
$$\int_0^2 p(x)\,dx = \tfrac13\big(p(0) + 4p(1) + p(2)\big)\quad\text{for every } p\in\mathcal{P}_2.$$
This is Simpson's rule; the dual basis explains why three weights suffice and how to find them.

blocks.title: An annihilator and a quotient in $\mathbb{R}^4$
blocks.body: Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^4$ be spanned by $u_1 = (1,0,1,0)$ and $u_2 = (0,1,1,1)$. Find a basis of $U^0$, and use it to identify $\mathbb{R}^4/U$ with $\mathbb{R}^2$.
blocks.solution:
A functional $\varphi(x) = ax_1+bx_2+cx_3+dx_4$ kills $U$ iff $a + c = 0$ and $b+c+d=0$. Choosing $(c,d) = (1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ gives the basis
$$\varphi_1 = (-1,-1,1,0),\qquad \varphi_2 = (0,-1,0,1)$$
of $U^0$, which has dimension $4-2=2$ as predicted.

Now let $T:\mathbb{R}^4\to\mathbb{R}^2$, $T(x) = (\varphi_1(x),\varphi_2(x))$. Its null space contains $U$, and has dimension $4 - \operatorname{rank}T = 2$ since $\varphi_1,\varphi_2$ are independent; so $\operatorname{null}T = U$ and $T$ is onto. By the first isomorphism theorem $\mathbb{R}^4/U \cong \mathbb{R}^2$, with coset $x+U$ corresponding to $(\varphi_1(x),\varphi_2(x))$. For instance $(1,1,2,1) = u_1+u_2$ is in $U$, and indeed $T(1,1,2,1) = (0,0)$.

blocks.title: When does one functional depend on others?
blocks.body: Let $\varphi, \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_k$ be linear functionals on any vector space $V$ (not necessarily finite-dimensional). Prove that if every $v$ with $\varphi_1(v) = \dots = \varphi_k(v) = 0$ also satisfies $\varphi(v) = 0$, then $\varphi = c_1\varphi_1+\dots+c_k\varphi_k$ for some scalars $c_i$.
blocks.solution:
Define $T: V \to F^k$ by $T(v) = (\varphi_1(v),\dots,\varphi_k(v))$. The hypothesis says $\operatorname{null}T \subseteq \operatorname{null}\varphi$. So $\varphi$ is constant on cosets of $\operatorname{null}T$ and induces a functional $\bar\varphi$ on $V/\operatorname{null}T$. By the first isomorphism theorem $V/\operatorname{null}T \cong \operatorname{range}T \subseteq F^k$, so $\bar\varphi$ becomes a linear functional $\chi$ on the subspace $\operatorname{range}T$, with $\varphi = \chi\circ T$.

Extend $\chi$ to all of $F^k$ (extend a basis of $\operatorname{range}T$ to a basis of $F^k$ and send the new vectors to $0$). Every functional on $F^k$ has the form $y \mapsto c_1y_1+\dots+c_ky_k$, so $\varphi(v) = \chi(T v) = \sum_i c_i\varphi_i(v)$. The finite-dimensional space here is $F^k$, not $V$, which is why the result holds for every $V$. This lemma is the linear-algebra core of the method of Lagrange multipliers.

blocks.body:
- $V$ and $V^*$ have the same dimension in finite dimensions, but there is no basis-free isomorphism between them; on a real inner product space, $v\mapsto\langle\cdot,v\rangle$ is one ([[inner-products]]).
- The dual functional $\varphi_j$ is not determined by $v_j$ alone; it changes if the other basis vectors change.
- In infinite dimensions the "dual basis" does not span $V^*$ and $V \to V^{**}$ is not onto.
- A coset $v+U$ with $v\notin U$ is not a subspace (it does not contain $0$); it is the element of $V/U$, and the zero element of $V/U$ is the coset $U$ itself.
- The dual map goes backwards, $T': W^*\to V^*$, and $(ST)' = T'S'$ reverses order, just as $(AB)^{\mathsf{T}} = B^{\mathsf{T}}A^{\mathsf{T}}$.

Dual spaces are the starting point of multilinear algebra: bilinear forms are elements of $(V\otimes V)^*$ and tensors of type $(p,q)$ mix copies of $V$ and $V^*$ ([[tensor-products]]). In analysis one keeps only continuous functionals, and the [[hahn-banach]] theorem guarantees that there are enough of them; on a Hilbert space they are all inner products with a fixed vector ([[hilbert-spaces]]). The cotangent vectors and the differential forms of [[differential-forms]] are dual objects, and the quotient construction is the linear version of the quotient groups of [[group-homomorphisms]] and quotient rings of [[rings]].

1. Find the dual basis of $(1,0,0), (1,1,0), (1,1,1)$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
2. Find weights $a,b$ such that $\int_{-1}^1 p(x)\,dx = a\,p(-1/\sqrt3) + b\,p(1/\sqrt3)$ for every polynomial $p$ of degree at most $1$, and check that the formula still holds for degree $3$.
3. Prove that $T$ is injective if and only if $T'$ is surjective, for $T$ between finite-dimensional spaces.
4. Let $U$ be the subspace of $\mathcal{P}_3$ of polynomials with $p(1)=p'(1)=0$. What is $\dim \mathcal{P}_3/U$, and which functionals on $\mathcal{P}_3$ give coordinates on it?
